tier_reason: First-party doc docs/docs.en/Performance.md lists the full Google Benchmark program, Clang 13 and the CPU (Xeon Platinum 8163), but no optimisation flags, standard library or folly/cppcoro versions, and the repo's benchmarks/Lazy.bench.cpp holds only the async_simple rows, so it falls short of A; first-party with partial methodology is C.

corrections.caveats: First-party document whose own closing note says the test is a simple one and does not mean async_simple is better, and adds that folly's Task has more functionality (it records context on each switch for debuggability), so the folly gap partly reflects that feature cost. Flags (-O level), libstdc++/libc++ choice and baseline library versions are missing, so it falls short of tier A. Only task creation, call-chain and fan-out speed are measured, not real I/O or an executor, because the doc says async_simple has no production-grade executor. Doc was last edited 2023-03-24 (file created 2022-02-21) and numbers are from Clang 13. The benchmark source in the repo (benchmarks/Lazy.bench.cpp) contains only the async_simple rows (plus RescheduleLazy variants); folly and cppcoro rows exist only in the doc's listing. Against cppcoro the margin is within a few percent on the chain case (about 1.03x). std::async is not benchmarked. The repo's other published comparisons (docs/docs.en/QuantitativeAnalysisReportOfCoroutinePerformance.md, Xeon E5-2650 v2, Google Benchmark) compare Lazy only with the project's own stackful Uthread (about 100x faster switching), and docs/docs.en/ImproveNetLibWithAsyncSimple.md shows a coroutine HTTP server at 72363 qps vs a blocking server at 32483 qps (2.2x, Xeon E5-2682 v4, wrk); neither names a listed baseline. Maintainer discussion #309 estimates a coroutine switch costs about 10 ns (estimate, not a measurement).

notes: All six Time values and the derived ratios (3.3x, 1.03x, 3.0x, 1.13x) match the doc; file history (Init 2022-02-21, last edit 2023-03-24) and repo metadata (Apache-2.0, 2.2k stars, last commit 2026-09-13, not archived) check out. Only change: caveat now cites the doc's own remark that folly Task does extra context recording.

tier_reason: Independent third-party suite (Vector's public vector-test-harness, run by a competitor whose own product loses this case) shows Fluent Bit 20.5 MiB/s vs Fluentd 2.6 and Logstash 4.6 MiB/s with public configs and AWS instance types, but prebuilt packages mean no compiler/flags and no exact CPU model, so not A.

corrections.hardware: AWS EC2: subject c5.large (2 vCPU), five c5.large producers and a c5d.xlarge consumer for the regex case (cases/regex_parsing_performance/configurations/default/terraform.tfvars); subject c5.large and consumer c5.xlarge for file-to-TCP multi_file (cases/file_to_tcp_performance/configurations/multi_file/terraform.tfvars). Exact CPU model not stated.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 8.2k stars; CNCF graduated (Fluentd ecosystem); README says it is deployed over 10 million times daily and has passed 15 billion downloads
corrections.caveats: Measured by the Vector project (a competing log router) in its public test harness, not by Fluent Bit's authors; results are single runs without variance, and the same tables show Vector beating Fluent Bit on file-to-TCP (76.7 vs 35 MiB/s) and TCP-to-TCP. Instance types are public in the cases' configurations/*/terraform.tfvars (c5.large subject), but the exact CPU model is not given and packages are prebuilt, so no compiler or flags exist, hence not tier A. Subject configs are public (cases/regex_parsing_performance/ansible/config_files): every tool runs its default single process/worker with the same regex; Fluent Bit and Fluentd both peak at about 50% CPU user on the 2-vCPU subject (one core), Logstash uses grok and reaches 90.5%. In the regex case Fluent Bit used more memory than Fluentd (584.5 MiB vs 246.1 MiB peak), and Fluentd forwards with its msgpack forward protocol while Fluent Bit sends json_lines over TCP. Versions differ per case: the file-to-TCP table is from 2019 releases, the regex table was refreshed in the harness' 2026 refresh commit (#101, 2026-06-18); the Fluentd version label (4.5.2-1) looks like a td-agent package version, not the Fluentd core version (not checked against the harness bootstrap). The harness README warns it is under construction and not fully validated against recent versions. Fluent Bit's own documentation claim of roughly 650 KB idle memory vs about 40 MB for Fluentd (seen only as a search-result paraphrase) could not be opened because docs.fluentbit.io did not resolve; no Fluent Bit-run benchmark was reachable. The harness' TCP-to-HTTP and TCP-to-blackhole case pages were not opened; their Fluent Bit vs Fluentd figures (19.6 vs <1 MiB/s and 64.4 vs 27.7 MiB/s) were seen only in a copy of Vector's README performance table at https://github.com/appsignal/vector, which gives no hardware or versions.

notes: Regex table (20.5 / 2.6 / 4.6 MiB/s, versions 3.2.7 / 4.5.2-1 / 8.17.3) and file-to-TCP multi-file table (35 / 26.1 / 3.1 MiB/s, memory 370.3 / 890.6 / 763.7 MiB) match the harness READMEs. Record wrongly said instance types were not public: default tfvars name c5.large subjects, so hardware is filled in. Repo metadata (Apache-2.0, 8.2k stars, last commit 2026-10-24, not archived) checks out.
